title: CPA Tumors: The Neuro-Ophthalmic Nexus
summary: Cerebellopontine Angle (CPA) tumors are critical lesions that compress cranial nerves VI, VII, and VIII, demanding a multidisciplinary approach for management and vision preservation. This poster details the clinical progression from hearing loss to complex ocular motility and facial nerve deficits.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: A Cerebellopontine Angle (CPA) tumor is a neoplasm located in the potential space between the cerebellum and the pons. While Vestibular Schwannomas (Acoustic Neuromas) are most common, the clinical hallmark of CPA syndrome is the progressive involvement of the V, VI, VII, and VIII cranial nerves as the tumor expands from the internal auditory canal (IAC) toward the brainstem.

sections.title: The 'Seven-Six-Five' Progression
content: Step 1: CN VIII - Tinnitus, high-frequency hearing loss, and vertigo.
Step 2: CN VII - Progressive Lower Motor Neuron facial weakness and gustatory changes.
Step 3: CN V - Reduced corneal sensation (an early, subtle sign of enlargement).
Step 4: CN VI - Lateral rectus palsy leading to esotropia and horizontal diplopia.
Step 5: Brainstem/Cerebellum - Ataxia, nystagmus, and signs of increased ICP.

rows: Eccentric to IAC, broad dural base
Slow hearing loss, NF2 if bilateral
Pearly white on surgery, slow growth

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: CN VI Palsy: Failure of abduction, esotropia worse at distance.
CN VII Palsy: Lagophthalmos, ectropion, and loss of the blink reflex.
CN V Involvement: Absent or diminished corneal sensation (test with cotton wisp).
Nystagmus: Bruns nystagmus (large-amplitude, slow-frequency toward lesion).
Papilledema: If the tumor causes obstructive hydrocephalus.
Exposure Keratopathy: Secondary to combined VII and V nerve dysfunction.

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Sudden onset headache with nausea (Hydrocephalus)
Bilateral CPA tumors (Pathognomonic for NF2)
Rapidly progressive ophthalmoplegia
Profound corneal anesthesia with lagophthalmos (High risk for perforation)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: 1. Pure Tone Audiometry: To document sensorineural hearing loss and speech discrimination.
2. Gadolinium-Enhanced MRI (Gold Standard): Focus on IAC and posterior fossa.
3. CT Temporal Bone: If bony erosion or anatomy of the semi-circular canals is needed for surgery.
4. Corneal Esthesiometry: Objective measurement of V1 trigeminal involvement.
5. Automated Perimetry: If papilledema is suspected (blind spot enlargement).

rows: Tumor protrudes into CPA; no brainstem contact
Tumor displaces brainstem and cranial nerves

sections.title: Ophthalmic Management Protocol
content: 1. Lubrication: Preservative-free tears every 1-2 hours.
2. Moisture Chambers: At night or for severe exposure.
3. Punctal Occlusion: For chronic dry eye management.
4. Upper Lid Gold Weight: To aid gravity-assisted closure.
5. Botulinum Toxin: Temporary protective ptosis.
6. Prism Therapy: For CN VI esotropia if stable.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Hitselberger's Sign: Hypesthesia of the posterior external auditory canal (early CN VII sign).
Crocodile Tears: Gustolacrimal reflex can occur during regeneration after CN VII palsy.
The 'Dangerous Combo': The combination of CN VII palsy and CN V anesthesia leads to rapid corneal melt.
NF2: Always check for posterior subcapsular cataracts (PSC) in suspected NF2 patients.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Bevacizumab in NF2
sections.content: Recent landmark studies have shown that Bevacizumab (Avastin), an anti-VEGF agent, can induce tumor shrinkage and improve hearing in patients with Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2) who have progressive vestibular schwannomas that are not amenable to surgery or radiation.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Permanent Facial Paralysis (10-30% depending on size).
CSF Leaks (Rhinorrhea or Otorrhea).
Tinnitus (Persistent in 50%).
Corneal Scarring/Perforation due to neurotrophic keratopathy.
Vascular stroke (AICA or PICA territory).

content.explanation: Afferent: Trigeminal Nerve (V1). Efferent: Facial Nerve (Orbicularis oculi). In CPA tumors, both can be damaged, abolishing the blink entirely.
